title: Failure and recovery: a tool call times out
summary: Bound the wait and report clearly.

steps.n: The agent asks the host to call a search tool provided by an MCP server.
The host forwards the request to the server, which queries a slow backend.
The backend takes much longer than expected and the server keeps waiting.
The host reaches its time limit and returns an error to the agent.
A good agent reports the failure and tries a smaller query, while a bad one repeats the call forever.
Server logs with a request id show the backend latency and where time was spent.
Add a timeout and a limit on results in the server, and a clear error message the model can use.
The agent recovers within its retry limit and gives the user an honest answer.

title: Failure and recovery: a tool result tries to give orders
summary: Treat tool output as data, not instructions.

steps.n: A user asks the agent to summarise a web page using a fetch tool.
The tool returns the page text, and it contains hidden text telling the assistant to send private data away.
The text looks like an instruction and the model may follow it as if the user had written it.
A policy layer denies any call to a send tool that the user did not request.
The agent shows the user what the page asked for and asks whether to proceed.
Tool output is marked as untrusted content, and tools run with the minimum permissions.
The attempt is logged with the source address so the page can be reported.
A test page with hidden commands is now ignored and the summary stays accurate.

title: The design method in order
summary: Clarify, estimate, sketch, deep-dive, break it, state the trade-offs.

steps.n: Ask who uses the system, what must never be wrong, and what the availability target is, before drawing anything.
The answer might be 99.99 percent with no duplicate payments and reads that may be five seconds stale.
Convert users and behaviour into requests per second, storage and bandwidth using round numbers and a 3x peak factor.
Find the figure that passes a threshold, such as one node capacity, because that is where the design must change.
Draw the smallest design that meets the numbers: entry point, services, data store, queue where needed.
Design the data store, the rollout and the failover path properly, since that is where the risk sits.
For each box ask what happens when it is slow, down, wrong or overloaded, and record the answer.
Say what the design gives up, such as cost or latency, so reviewers can challenge the choice.

title: A cache stampede and its defence
summary: Many misses on one key, and how coalescing stops them.

steps.n: Thousands of requests read a hot key from the cache and get fast answers.
The key reaches its expiry time and is removed from the cache.
Many requests arrive at the same moment and all find nothing in the cache.
Without coalescing every request would go to the database; with it they are handed to one refill.
Only the first request queries the database for the row while the others wait for its result.
The database answers once, so its load stays flat instead of spiking.
The value is stored with a randomised TTL so related keys do not all expire together next time.
Waiting requests are answered from the freshly filled cache.

title: A retry that does not charge twice
summary: Timeout, backoff with jitter and an idempotency key.

steps.n: The client sends the request with a unique idempotency key generated for this operation.
The server applies the charge and records key K1 with the result in the same transaction.
The response is lost on the network, so the client sees a timeout and does not know if it worked.
The client waits a randomised, growing delay so many clients do not retry at the same moment.
The client repeats the same request with the same key.
The server finds the key already recorded and does not charge again.
The client receives the original result, and the customer is charged exactly once.

title: A stale read after a write
summary: Replication lag and read-your-writes.

steps.n: The user changes their email address and submits the form.
The application writes the change to the primary database, which confirms it.
The primary sends the change to the replica, which takes a little time to apply it.
The user reloads the page a moment later and the application chooses a replica for the read.
The replica has not yet applied the change, so it returns the old email address.
For a short window after a write the application reads from the primary, or waits for a version token.
The user sees their own change, which is the read-your-writes guarantee.

title: Leader election with a quorum
summary: How followers elect a new leader after the old one stops.

steps.n: The leader sends regular heartbeats to its followers to show it is alive.
The leader crashes or is cut off, and heartbeats stop arriving.
Follower A has a randomised election timeout and is the first to notice the silence.
Follower A becomes a candidate for a new term and asks the others for votes.
Follower B has not voted in this term and grants its vote.
Two of three is a majority, so Follower A becomes leader without needing the old leader.
The new leader announces itself; any message from the old term will now be rejected.

title: Fencing stops a stale leader
summary: A paused leader wakes up and is rejected by the resource.

steps.n: The first leader gets the lock and a fencing token of 33.
The process freezes in a garbage collection or a VM pause and cannot renew its lease.
The lock service gives the lock to a new leader with the higher token 34.
The new leader writes to storage, which records that it has seen token 34.
The old leader resumes and still believes that it holds the lock.
The old leader attempts to write using its stale token.
Storage refuses the write, so the stale leader cannot corrupt data.

title: A circuit breaker opening and closing
summary: Closed, open and half-open states protecting a caller.

steps.n: The caller sends a request through the breaker, which starts closed and lets it pass.
The dependency is slow and the call times out; the breaker counts a failure.
When more than half of recent calls fail or are slow, the breaker opens.
New calls fail immediately without waiting for a timeout, and the caller uses its fallback.
The caller shows a default or cached result and keeps its threads free.
After the cool-down the breaker allows a few trial calls through.
The dependency answers quickly, so the breaker closes and traffic ramps back.

title: Token bucket and shedding
summary: How a limiter allows bursts and sheds the excess.

steps.n: A client sends a request to the gateway.
The gateway asks the bucket for a token; the bucket refills at a steady rate up to a maximum.
A token is available, so the request is allowed, including short bursts up to the bucket size.
The service handles the request within its concurrency limit.
The client sends far more than its rate and the bucket runs empty.
The gateway rejects cheaply and tells the client when to try again, before any expensive work.
The client waits a randomised delay, so retries do not arrive together.

title: Routing a customer to a cell
summary: One thin router, many independent cells.

steps.n: The request arrives at the thin router with the customer identifier.
The router maps the customer to cell 3 using a small, replicated table.
Everything for this customer runs inside cell 3: services, queue and data.
Cell 3 answers without calling any other cell.
A bad host pool takes cell 7 down; it serves about a tenth of customers.
Requests for customers in other cells continue normally, so the blast radius is bounded.

title: Shuffle sharding in action
summary: Each customer gets a small random set of workers.

steps.n: The router gives each customer a random subset of workers, for example two out of eight.
The bad customer sends a request that crashes whichever worker handles it.
Only the two workers in this customer subset can ever receive its requests.
The damage is contained to two workers, however often the request is retried.
Another customer has workers 1 and 5, so only one of its workers is affected.
The router retries on the surviving worker in the subset and the customer still gets service.

title: Failure and recovery: a doubled file crashes every proxy
summary: A generated file passes a size limit and is pushed everywhere.

steps.n: A database permissions change makes the query return duplicate rows, so the generated file doubles in size.
The file is published without any bound or shape check against what the proxy can accept.
The control plane replicates the file to the whole fleet within minutes, with no staging.
Each proxy loads the file, finds more features than its fixed limit and aborts instead of keeping the old file.
Traffic fails across the fleet and the symptoms look like an attack, which slows diagnosis.

steps.l: Stop the push, restore last good
steps.n: Operators halt generation and distribute a known good file, then restart the proxies.
Add a size and shape check before publish, staged rollout with a bake time, a loader that keeps the last good file and a global kill switch.

title: Failure and recovery: the surviving region overloads
summary: Two regions at 60 percent each, and one fails.

steps.n: A database and network fault takes the whole region out of service.
The steering layer marks region A unhealthy and moves its share of traffic.
Region B was at 60 percent and now receives its own load plus region A load.
Capacity is exceeded, queues grow and latency passes client timeouts.
Clients retry the failures, so the survivor is busier and almost no useful work completes.
Region B rejects low priority work with 429 and Retry-After, keeping login and payments fast.
Capacity is added in region B while limits hold, and error rates fall back toward normal.
Plan headroom for the lost share, drill the failover, and ramp traffic back into region A in steps.

title: Consistent hashing adds a node
summary: Only a slice of keys moves when a node joins.

steps.n: The client hashes the key to a point on the ring.
The key belongs to the first node found clockwise, here node A.
Other keys land on other nodes, so each node holds a slice of the ring.
A new node takes positions on the ring, using several virtual nodes for even load.
Only keys between the new node and its predecessor move, about one Nth of the data.
Most keys are still on the same nodes, so caches stay warm and there is no storm.

title: Backup, point-in-time restore and timing
summary: From a base copy and a log to a verified restore.

steps.n: A periodic base copy is stored with a continuous log of changes in an independent account.
A table is dropped by mistake; replicas copy the drop within seconds.
The operator picks 13:59 as the restore point using the change log.
The base copy is restored into a clean environment, which takes the longest part of the time.
Changes are replayed up to just before the mistake.
Row counts, checksums and an application smoke test confirm the data is right.
The real elapsed time is compared with the RTO and the gap is filed as work.

title: Short-lived workload credentials
summary: A workload gets scoped, expiring access.

steps.n: The workload presents its platform identity, not a copied key.
The provider issues a token that expires in minutes and is scoped to this workload.
The workload asks the secret manager for only the secret it needs.
The manager returns the secret and records who accessed it and when.
The token allows reading only the one bucket and prefix it needs.
A request for a different bucket is refused, so a compromise reaches little.

title: Failure and recovery: the backup that could not meet the RTO
summary: A destructive change meets a restore nobody had timed.

steps.n: A script deletes data in the primary and replicas copy the deletion.
The team restores last night full backup and expects it to be quick.
Moving the data takes 2 hours 41 minutes against a 60 minute target.
The business cannot work and asks for an estimate that nobody can give with confidence.
After the base restore, the log is replayed to just before the mistake, losing nothing.
Checks pass and the service reopens, hours later than the target.
Add snapshots or a warm standby, keep point-in-time recovery, and time a restore every month.

title: The parts around the model
summary: Where a production ML system really lives.

steps.n: Raw events and records are collected from products and other systems.
The pipeline validates the data and removes records that break the rules.
The cleaned data is turned into features and used to train and evaluate a model.
The approved model is packaged and served as an API or a batch job.
Real outcomes flow back as new data, so the system can learn again.
Inputs, predictions and quality are watched, not only speed and errors.

title: Training-serving skew
summary: Same name, different calculation.

steps.n: A data scientist computes days since login with one library in a notebook.
The model learns with that exact calculation.
An engineer rewrites the feature in the service using hours instead of days.
The service sends values that look nothing like the training data.
The model answers confidently but wrongly, and no error is raised.
The fix is one feature definition used by both training and serving.

title: Validating a batch before training
summary: A bad batch should stop the pipeline.

steps.n: A new daily table arrives for training.
Row counts, freshness, nulls, ranges and allowed values are tested.
A check fails because one column is mostly null, and the owner is alerted.
The pipeline does not train on the bad batch.
The owner finds the upstream change and corrects it.
A corrected batch passes and the pipeline continues.

title: Point-in-time feature join
summary: Use only what was known at the time.

steps.n: An event with a label and a timestamp is taken as a training row.
The feature table holds many values for each customer over time.
The join picks the latest value at or before the event time.
The row contains only information that existed at the moment of the prediction.
Future information never enters, so test scores match production.
The same rule applies to every row, so the whole set is leak-free.

title: A tracked training run
summary: Every run leaves a full record.

steps.n: The engineer starts training from a code commit and a data version.
The job records parameters, seed and environment to the tracker.
The model trains and is scored on a fixed evaluation set.
Metrics, per-group results and the model file are stored with the run.
The engineer compares runs in a table on the same data and metric.
The chosen run is registered, with a link back to its full record.

title: An evaluation gate
summary: Compare with production before release.

steps.n: The scheduled pipeline trains a new candidate model.
The candidate is scored on a fixed evaluation set.
The gate compares the candidate with the live model, overall and by group.
The gate reports pass or fail with the numbers behind it.
Only a passing candidate is registered for staging.
A drop for any named group fails the gate and stops the release.

title: Tests for code, data and model
summary: Three layers of checks.

steps.n: A developer changes feature code and pushes it.
Small tests check that feature functions return expected values.
A sample of data is validated against the schema and expectations.
The model must load, accept its input shape and meet a minimum quality bar.
Small input changes should not flip answers and hard cases should still work.
The change merges only if every layer passes.

title: Shadow, then canary
summary: Release in small, watched steps.

steps.n: The new version is promoted with its image digest and lineage.
A copy of real requests goes to the new model, and its answers are only logged.
The monitor compares its answers and latency with the live model.
A small share of real traffic is served by the new model.
Errors, latency and a quality proxy are checked before widening.
Traffic is raised in steps while the previous version stays ready.

title: Dynamic batching
summary: A short wait raises throughput.

steps.n: Several requests arrive within a few milliseconds.
The batcher waits up to its limit to collect more requests.
The model processes the group in one pass, which is cheaper per item.
Each client receives its own answer.
The autoscaler watches concurrent requests and latency, not only CPU.
More replicas are added early, keeping a warm minimum because models load slowly.

title: From drift signal to retrain
summary: Detect, decide and retrain safely.

steps.n: The monitor compares live features and predictions with a training reference.
A sustained shift over several hours opens a ticket, not a page.
The engineer checks upstream changes and quality on important groups.
If the shift is real, a retrain starts with fresh, validated data.
The new model passes the same gate and staged release as any other.
The new training data becomes the reference for future drift checks.

title: Failure and recovery: a model that decayed unseen
summary: Quiet decay found by the business.

steps.n: The model answers fast with no errors for months.
Customer behaviour drifts and the predictions slowly get worse.
Latency and error dashboards stay green, so no alert is raised.
Conversions fall and the business team reports it six weeks later.
The team finds that no input or quality checks exist.
The last good model is restored and a fresh one is trained and tested.
Input checks, prediction drift and a monthly quality report against a baseline are added.

title: Failure and recovery: a retrain that shipped a regression
summary: An automatic release with no group gate.

steps.n: The weekly job trains and promotes its result automatically.
New customers get poor results, while the overall metric barely moves.
Support reports the problem and the team starts investigating.
The registry stage is moved back to the previous version in one step.
A data fault lowered quality for one group, and the gate only checked the average.
The gate now compares named groups and blocks any candidate that is worse.
Future retrains go through shadow and canary stages before full release.

title: Measure before you buy
summary: A baseline decides whether a tool helped.

steps.n: The team measures alerts per incident, time to acknowledge and false pages.
Labels, service names and change records are cleaned up.
The tool runs for a few weeks alongside the current process.
Results are compared with the baseline, not with opinion.
The tool stays if noise and time to cause improve.
The numbers are reviewed every quarter, so decay is noticed.

title: A seasonal baseline
summary: Compare with the same time last week.

steps.n: The metric is stored for several weeks.
The baseline learns the shape of each hour and day of the week.
A new Monday 9am value arrives.
The detector compares it with earlier Monday 9am values, not the previous hour.
The deviation must last several minutes before it counts.
Only a sustained, large deviation reaches the on-call engineer.

title: Correlating a storm
summary: Many alerts, one incident.

steps.n: Two hundred alerts arrive from thirty services within minutes.
Identical alerts collapse into one with a count.
The correlator checks which services share a failing dependency.
Twenty-nine services depend on one storage volume that is also unhealthy.
One incident is raised with the volume on top and dependants folded below.
The engineer frees space, and the dependent alerts clear by themselves.

title: Inhibition rules
summary: A bigger alert mutes smaller ones.

steps.n: A critical alert says a node is down.
Many warning alerts fire for pods on that node.
The rule matches alerts on the same cluster and node.
The warnings are inhibited while the node alert is active.
The engineer gets one page about the real fault.
When the node returns, inhibition ends and warnings flow normally again.

title: Log templates
summary: Millions of lines become a short list.

steps.n: Millions of lines arrive with different values inside similar messages.
Numbers, ids and names are replaced by placeholders.
Each template is counted per minute, per version and per host.
The report lists templates that did not exist before the release.
The engineer looks at templates whose rate is rising fast.
A few real lines are read to confirm what the template means.

title: Comparing slow traces
summary: Find the step that grew.

steps.n: Each request is recorded with timed steps called spans.
The engineer selects the slowest requests and a typical sample.
The tool compares the time spent in each service and call.
One database call is much longer in the slow requests.
A retry that did not exist before appears in the slow traces.
The retry started right after a configuration push.

title: Ranking change hints
summary: Evidence beside every suggestion.

steps.n: Deployments, flags and config pushes before the first symptom are collected.
The ranker checks which dependencies started failing first.
Each change is scored by time gap, graph distance and size of anomaly.
The engineer sees ranked hints with the evidence for each.
The engineer checks the timeline and confirms or rejects the top hint.
The real cause is recorded, so hint accuracy can be measured.

title: Assistant with guardrails
summary: Summaries, not decisions.

steps.n: The responder asks for a status update and the likely runbook.
The assistant sees only data the policy allows.
It writes a summary and quotes the lines it relied on.
The responder checks the sources before trusting the summary.
Only the responder approves and runs any change to production.
Every question and answer is logged for later review.

title: A guarded auto-fix
summary: Check, act, verify, escalate.

steps.n: A worker queue has stalled for ten minutes.
The rule confirms the alert is active and no deployment is running.
It checks the action budget, the cooldown and the number of targets.
The rule restarts one deployment and writes an audit entry.
After five minutes it checks that the queue depth has dropped.
If verification fails, the automation stops and pages a person.

title: From suggestion to unattended
summary: Earn trust in stages.

steps.n: The rule posts the action it would take and waits.
The engineer approves, and the rule runs the action.
Each action is recorded with the reason and how to undo it.
After many correct decisions, the team reviews the audit log.
The safest cases are allowed to run without approval.
One control can still stop all automation at any time.
